title: Reported speech 2
subtitle: He said that his job is boring.
summary: Decide when the verb has to change in reported speech, use say and tell correctly, and report orders and requests with tell/ask somebody to do something.

lesson.heading: You don't always have to change the verb
lesson.text: If the situation is still the same, it is not necessary to change the verb to the past. Both forms are correct.

examples.text: *reported:* Paul said that his new job **is** boring.
examples.note: his job is still boring now

examples.text: *reported:* Paul said that his new job **was** boring.
Helen told me that she **wants** to go to Canada next year.

lesson.heading: When the situation has changed or finished
lesson.text: If the situation has changed or finished, you **need** a past verb.

examples.text: *direct:* Paul left the room suddenly. He said, 'I **have to** go.'
*reported:* Paul left the room suddenly. He said that he **had to** go.

lesson.heading: When what was said is not really true
lesson.text: You also need the past in reported speech when what was said is different from what is really true. A few days ago Rachel told you: *'Have you heard? Joe is in hospital.'* Later that day you meet Joe in the street:

examples.text: Joe, this is a surprise. Rachel said you **were** in hospital.

lesson.heading: say and tell

left.label: tell somebody
left.text: Use tell when you say who somebody is talking to.
examples: Rachel **told me** that you were in hospital.
Dan **told me** that he was bored with his job.

right.label: say
right.text: Use say when you do not mention the listener.
examples: Rachel **said** that you were in hospital.
Anna **said goodbye to me** and left.

lesson.note: not ~~Rachel said me~~ and not ~~Rachel told that ...~~

lesson.heading: tell/ask somebody to do something
lesson.text: We say **tell somebody to ...** and **ask somebody to ...** . For orders and requests, this is usually more natural than a that-clause. The negative is **not to ...** .

examples.text: 'Drink plenty of water,' the doctor said to me. - The doctor **told me to drink** plenty of water.
'Don't work too hard,' I said to Joe. - I **told Joe not to work** too hard.
'Can you help me, please,' Jackie said to me. - Jackie **asked me to help** her.
Paul **said not to worry** about him.

lesson.text: Simple rule for say and tell: tell needs a person straight after it (tell me, tell Kate); say does not (say something, say it to me).

exercises.prompt: Earlier Sarah said, 'I don't like fish.' Now she says, 'Let's have fish for dinner.' You reply: But you said ___ fish.
exercises.explanation: What she said is different from what is really true, so we need a past verb.

exercises.prompt: Earlier Sarah said, 'I can't drive.' Now she says, 'I'm going to buy a car.' You reply: But you said ___.
exercises.explanation: can't becomes couldn't in reported speech.

exercises.prompt: Earlier Sarah said, 'Jane has a very well-paid job.' Now she says, 'Jane is always short of money.' You reply: But you said ___ a very well-paid job.
exercises.explanation: has becomes had, because what she said does not match the real situation.

exercises.prompt: A few days ago Rachel told you that Joe was in hospital. Today you meet Joe in the street. What do you say?
options: Rachel said you were in hospital.
Rachel said you are in hospital.
Rachel told that you were in hospital.
exercises.explanation: Joe clearly isn't in hospital, so we use a past verb; and told always needs an object (told me).

exercises.prompt: Earlier Sarah said, 'I've never been to the United States.' Now she says, 'I think New York is a great place.' You reply: But you said ___ to the United States.
exercises.explanation: have/has becomes had, so I've never been becomes you'd never been.

exercises.prompt: Match each thing that was said with its reported form.

pairs.right: I told him to hurry up.
I asked her to slow down.
I told her not to worry.

pairs.left: 'Do you think you could give me a hand, Tom?'
pairs.right: I asked Tom to give me a hand.
I told him to mind his own business.
He asked her to marry him.

exercises.prompt: Don't ___ anybody what I said. It's a secret just between us.
exercises.explanation: anybody is the listener, and only tell can be followed straight by a person.

exercises.statement: Rachel said me that you were in hospital.
exercises.explanation: Rachel told me that you were in hospital. (or Rachel said that you were in hospital.) We never say 'said me'.

exercises.prompt: Which verb fits each gap - say or tell?

items.text: Anna ___ goodbye to me and left.
She ___ she would be here at 8 o'clock.
Gary couldn't help me. He ___ me to ask Chris.
The doctor ___ that I should rest for at least a week.

exercises.statement: Paul left the room suddenly. He said that he has to go.
exercises.explanation: He said that he had to go. The situation is finished, so we need a past verb.

exercises.prompt: Sarah was driving too fast, so you asked her about her speed. Report what you did.
exercises.answer: I asked her to slow down.
exercises.explanation: Requests are reported with ask somebody to do something.

exercises.prompt: Sue was nervous about the situation, so I told ___.
exercises.explanation: The negative of tell somebody to ... is tell somebody not to ... .
